ARTICLE BODY:

Recent reports from public health authorities and climate scientists estimate that Europe’s June heatwave resulted in thousands of deaths, though the specific figures vary depending on the calculation method used. According to [Q&A: Europe’s May and June heatwave deaths – and how they were counted](https://www.carbonbrief.org/qa-europes-may-and-june-heatwave-deaths-and-how-they-were-counted/), France’s national public health agency recorded 2,025 excess deaths during the week the heat peaked. In the same period, authorities in Germany and the Netherlands identified 5,753 and 533 excess deaths, respectively. Independent climate analysis suggests France saw more than 2,700 heat-related fatalities over 17 days in June. Separate research into the United Kingdom’s heat events identified 2,700 deaths, with 42% attributed to human-caused climate change. These discrepancies in counting arise because researchers utilize different analytical frameworks to quantify mortality, each balancing specific advantages and drawbacks.

## The Evolution of Mortality Metrics

Epidemiologists and economists have studied the correlation between rising temperatures and mortality for nearly a century. A 1923 study by geographer Ellsworth Huntington and economist Margaret Justin established that death rates in New York City rose sharply once temperatures exceeded 17C. As carbon emissions have driven global warming, scientists have increasingly connected these broader trends to individual events. By the 1990s, the 1995 Chicago heatwave became a focal point for detailed mortality analysis. Over the last decade, researchers have further refined this work by estimating how much human-influenced climate change contributes to specific death tolls. A 2016 study, for instance, found that human influence accounted for 506 of 735 summer deaths in Paris and 64 of 315 in London during a 2003 heatwave. Recent findings have quantified these links further, such as a 2018 Zurich study attributing 27% of heat-related deaths to global warming, and a 2021 British Columbia analysis assigning 11-15% of such deaths to the same cause.

## Methodological Divergence

Public health authorities currently rely on two primary, non-exclusive methods to estimate the human toll of heat. The "excess deaths" approach counts all fatalities during a heatwave that exceed a historical baseline for the same period. While this method allows authorities to produce rapid, high-impact estimates—such as the 32% increase in German deaths observed during the late June heatwave—it does not inherently isolate heat as the cause. Alternatively, statistical modelling uses long-term mortality data to determine the relationship between specific temperatures and death rates in a given region. This approach offers a more nuanced view but requires complex interdisciplinary expertise to run epidemiological models alongside counterfactual climate analyses. Death certificate coding, which explicitly records heatstroke as a cause of death, has fallen out of favor in many European jurisdictions because it fails to capture the full scope of heat-induced cardiovascular or respiratory failures.

## Implications for Public Health Data

The absence of a singular "ground truth" in mortality data mirrors the historical challenges of quantifying deaths from air pollution. While the scientific community has long accepted that particulate matter is toxic and lethal, the messaging surrounding heat-related mortality is more recent. Because high temperatures exacerbate chronic conditions like kidney injury, heart disease, and dementia, these deaths often appear on medical records as secondary or primary underlying causes rather than temperature-related incidents. As public health agencies continue to refine these methodologies, the reliance on models rather than certificates highlights a transition in how institutions monitor environmental risks. This shift indicates that the ability to track the human impact of a warming climate remains as much a project of statistical refinement as it is a process of public health reporting.
